title: Can you trust an answer that looks right?
summary: An AI assistant reads a number off a dataset, and it is correct. What did that prove? Our first video, with a professor, a student and Pulsar.

topic_data.hero_lead: An AI assistant hands back a number in the right format, in a confident tone, and it is correct. Our first video starts there and asks what that actually proved.

timeline.title: The sequence holds the shape
timeline.description: Anfinsen sets out the principle that a protein’s chain carries what it needs to fold. In principle, a shape can be predicted. In practice, not for decades.

timeline.title: CASP: predictions judged blind
timeline.description: A community experiment begins scoring structure predictions against experimental structures nobody has seen yet. The field builds checking into its institutions.

timeline.title: Foldit
timeline.description: A protein-folding game opens to the public. Its 2010 paper reports players matching or beating the leading algorithm on some puzzles: people and machines, checking each other.

timeline.title: AlphaFold at CASP14
timeline.description: Predictions “competitive with experimental structures in a majority of cases”. The result is believed because it was tested blind.

timeline.title: A confidence score on every residue
timeline.description: The AlphaFold database opens with pLDDT shown on each structure: a prediction that says where not to trust it.
timeline.short: A confidence score on every residue

timeline.title: Citations that look right
timeline.description: A study of ChatGPT literature reviews finds 55% of GPT-3.5 references and 18% of GPT-4 references fabricated, formatted like real ones.

timeline.title: A Nobel Prize for the field
timeline.description: The [Chemistry prize](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2024/summary/) goes to David Baker for computational protein design, and to Demis Hassabis and John Jumper for structure prediction.
timeline.short: A Nobel Prize for the field

topic_data.viewpoints_intro: We publish the strongest case against our own reading. If the objection is weak here, that is our failure, not the objection’s.

items.label: For checking
items.text: An assistant changes how fast drafts arrive, not who answers for them. A number in a report is the scientist’s claim, whoever produced it, and the scientist has to be able to say why it is right.
items.cite: The position the video leans toward
items.short: An assistant changes how fast drafts arrive, not who answers for them. A number in a report is the scientist’s claim, whoever produced it.

items.label: Against
items.text: If the assistant is right more often than a tired researcher at the end of a long week, a rule that its answers need checking is ritual, not rigour. Checks belong where errors are likely, and that includes the human ones.
items.cite: The strongest objection we could find

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Professor Hulse had spent thirty years studying proteins.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Tiny molecular machines inside living cells.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Their shapes determine what they can do. And if you can predict those shapes, you may be able to design better medicines.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: It was fascinating work.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Unfortunately, fascinating work does not usually care about your deadlines.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Hulse had forty-seven unread research papers, three unfinished lectures, and a simulation that had been running since Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: Hulse
transcript.text: Come on…

transcript.speaker: Hulse
transcript.text: Yes!

transcript.speaker: Hulse
transcript.text: …No.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The problem was not that Hulse disliked work.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The problem was that everything important had become urgent at the same time.

transcript.speaker: News anchor
transcript.text: New artificial intelligence methods are helping researchers analyze biological data and predict protein structures at unprecedented speed…

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Hulse had heard promises like this before.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Every few years, a new technology arrived promising to transform science.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: And every few years, Hulse discovered that the technology still needed someone to check whether it was wrong.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: But this time, the papers were different.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: AI was being used to recognize patterns in biological data, organize information, and explore possibilities that could take researchers years to investigate.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Hulse looked at his watch.

transcript.speaker: Hulse
transcript.text: If it can save me an afternoon…

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: For the first time, he began wondering whether AI could help him.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Not replace the science.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Just… help him get through the day.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Meanwhile, Taylor was having a much better week.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Taylor was one of those students who seemed to understand a problem before everyone else had finished explaining it.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Brilliant. Fast. Very good at finding patterns.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: And, apparently, very good at getting things done.

transcript.speaker: Taylor
transcript.text: Okay. One more.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: But Taylor had a question.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: What would Professor Hulse think?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Because Taylor was using an AI assistant.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: And every useful answer came with a second thought:

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Is this actually correct?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Taylor knew that using AI was not the same as trusting it.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: And that distinction was becoming important.

transcript.speaker: Hulse
transcript.text: Taylor.

transcript.speaker: Taylor
transcript.text: Professor.

transcript.speaker: Hulse
transcript.text: You finished processing the dataset?

transcript.speaker: Taylor
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Hulse
transcript.text: The diagrams?

transcript.speaker: Taylor
transcript.text: Yeah.

transcript.speaker: Hulse
transcript.text: The literature summary?

transcript.speaker: Taylor
transcript.text: …Yaup.

transcript.speaker: Hulse
transcript.text: It is eleven in the morning.

transcript.speaker: Taylor
transcript.text: I know.

transcript.speaker: Hulse
transcript.text: How?

transcript.speaker: Taylor
transcript.text: I used an AI assistant.

transcript.speaker: Hulse
transcript.text: And you trust it?

transcript.speaker: Taylor
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Hulse
transcript.text: Good.

transcript.speaker: Taylor
transcript.text: I trust it enough to ask questions.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: That answer interested Hulse.

transcript.speaker: Hulse
transcript.text: Show me how it works.

transcript.speaker: Taylor
transcript.text: Hi, Pulsar.

transcript.speaker: Pulsar
transcript.text: Good morning, Taylor. What can I do for you today?

transcript.speaker: Taylor
transcript.text: Pulsar, meet Professor Hulse. Please explain to him how you can help us with our research studies.

transcript.speaker: Pulsar
transcript.text: Professor Hulse. I have access to the research notes, documents, and datasets you have uploaded. I can analyze them, modify, and produce outputs according to your instructions. I can also review the literature, summarize, and create automated research reports.

transcript.speaker: Hulse
transcript.text: Can you answer only based on the files I provide?

transcript.speaker: Pulsar
transcript.text: Yes, if you provide the files and explicitly ask me to only use them, I will restrict my answers to their contents. I won’t use outside sources unless you give permission.

transcript.speaker: Hulse
transcript.text: Good. Then answer this.

transcript.speaker: Hulse
transcript.text: What is the molecular weight of the protein in yesterday’s dataset?

transcript.speaker: Pulsar
transcript.text: The molecular weight is approximately 9.8.

transcript.speaker: Hulse
transcript.text: Correct.

transcript.speaker: Taylor
transcript.text: I told you.

transcript.speaker: Hulse
transcript.text: That proves you can read a number.

transcript.speaker: Pulsar
transcript.text: That is correct.

transcript.speaker: Hulse
transcript.text: You agree?

transcript.speaker: Pulsar
transcript.text: Reading a number is not sufficient evidence of scientific reliability.

transcript.speaker: Hulse
transcript.text: …Interesting.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Hulse had expected a machine that sounded confident.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Instead, he found one that sounded almost annoyingly reasonable.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Which, in his experience, was a good sign.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: They started small.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: No revolutionary discoveries.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: No “Pulsar, solve cancer.”

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Just the ordinary work that quietly eats an entire researcher’s day.

transcript.speaker: Taylor
transcript.text: Pulsar, identify missing values and inconsistent formatting.

transcript.speaker: Pulsar
transcript.text: I found twelve missing entries and three inconsistent naming conventions. I have marked them for review.

transcript.speaker: Hulse
transcript.text: Summarize these papers. Focus on methods, limitations, and experimental evidence.

transcript.speaker: Pulsar
transcript.text: I can organize the findings. I will also distinguish between experimental results and the authors’ interpretations.

transcript.speaker: Hulse
transcript.text: Organize these simulation results by predicted stability.

transcript.speaker: Pulsar
transcript.text: I can do that. I can also identify which results require further validation.

transcript.speaker: Hulse
transcript.text: Do it.

transcript.speaker: Hulse
transcript.text: I need a diagram explaining protein folding for first-year students.

transcript.speaker: Pulsar
transcript.text: Would you prefer a simplified molecular model or a step-by-step visual explanation?

transcript.speaker: Hulse
transcript.text: Step-by-step.

transcript.speaker: Hulse
transcript.text: That is… actually good.

transcript.speaker: Taylor
transcript.text: Actually?

transcript.speaker: Hulse
transcript.text: Very good.

transcript.speaker: Hulse
transcript.text: I can see my desk.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The work had not disappeared.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: But the friction had.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: And that was enough to make the future look suddenly…

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Manageable.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: And finally, they returned to the research.

exercise.title: Try It: Check the Answer
exercise.intro: An assistant answered five questions about the dataset below. All five look right. For each one, accept it or check it against the table.
exercise.caption: Yesterday’s dataset. Invented for this exercise.

answers.question: What is the molecular weight of protein A?
answers.verdict: Right. It read a value off row A, which is exactly what Hulse said it proves: that it can read a number.

answers.question: Which protein is the most heat-stable?
answers.answer: Protein B, with the highest melting point at 72 °C.
answers.verdict: Wrong. Protein D melts at 81 °C. A comparison is a conclusion, and conclusions are where a fluent answer and a correct one part ways.

answers.question: How heavy is protein C?
answers.verdict: Wrong by a factor of a thousand. The table says 17.0 kDa. The number was read correctly; the unit was not.

answers.question: How many residues does protein F have?
answers.verdict: Right. Another value read straight off the table.

answers.question: Has anyone published on protein E’s stability?
answers.answer: Yes: Moreau and Lind (2019), Journal of Protein Stability, 12(3), 211–224.
answers.verdict: Made up, and formatted perfectly. Nothing in your files mentions it, and protein E itself is invented. A source from outside what you provided is always a check.

exercise.result_missed: went into your report looking exactly like the right ones. Look again at what they have in common.
exercise.result_all_checked: Nothing got past you, and you checked everything, including the two answers that only read a value off the table. That is the afternoon Hulse was trying to win back.
exercise.result_good: Nothing wrong got past you, and you skipped a check that did not matter. That is the skill: check what compares, carries a unit, or points outside your files.

discussion.question: If an assistant has been right ninety-nine times in a row, what should make you check the hundredth?
discussion.corrections: None yet. Anything we get wrong is logged here, with what changed and when.
